blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Censoring occurs when a subject’s exact event time is not known. In right censoring, follow-up ends before the event: the study ends, or the subject is lost to follow-up. The true event time is known only to be greater than the observed time.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html:
A censored subject gives you partial information: event-free for at least this long. This differs from ordinary missing data (a value absent altogether, §15.4), because the censored value has a known lower bound. Right censoring is the form this book uses. Left censoring (the event happened before observation began, at an unknown time) and interval censoring (the event is known only to lie between two visits) need other methods.

Two features of real follow-up show in Figure 14.1. First, subjects enter at different calendar times (staggered entry). Analysis uses time since each subject’s own start, so every line is shifted back to zero (panel b). A late entrant is therefore censored earlier on the analysis scale even though the study ended on the same calendar day for everyone. Second, censoring has two routes: administrative censoring at the planned end of the study, and loss to follow-up partway through.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: In the conceptual 3-year CBHI study (§14.1), subjects fall into three groups: members who drop out during the study (exact time known); members still enrolled at study end (administratively censored); and members who move away and cannot be traced (censored at the last date they were known to be enrolled). In Figure 14.1, Household 4 moves away at 14 months. Households 5 and 6 join 10 and 18 months into the study, so the study’s end censors them at 26 and 18 months of follow-up.

blocks.alt: Right censoring with staggered entry and loss to follow-up
blocks.caption: Figure 14.1. Six households. (a) Calendar time: households join the scheme at different times, and the study ends at month 36 for all. (b) The same follow-up re-aligned to time since enrolment, the scale survival analysis uses. Crosses are dropouts; the open circle is a household lost to follow-up; arrows are households still enrolled at the end.

points.html: Standard methods assume non-informative censoring: those censored “should be as likely to have a subsequent event as those individuals who remain in the study” (Clark et al., 2003). It fails if, say, households on the verge of leaving the scheme are also the ones who stop answering the door.

A competing event is not ordinary censoring. An event that makes the outcome impossible (death, when the outcome is TB culture conversion) must not be treated as censored when you estimate the probability of the outcome; §14.8 shows why and what to do instead.
Moving away counts as censoring only if the household could still have dropped out afterwards, unseen. If moving ends membership by another route, it is a competing event (§14.8 revisits this).
